summary: Memory-bound case: amdclang's build is at reference headroom 1.12 to 1.21 (every element touched exactly once, no re-reads), so 1.5x was out of reach; the shipped state is 1.041x (240 pairs, CI 1.0345 to 1.0496; 1.060x at 60 pairs), at headroom 1.09 to 1.10. State 465fdc7b495abe86 is a source-level relaunch: instead of one workgroup per position with block (32, H) = 16 waves at H=32, it launches cdiv(P*H, 2) one-wave workgroups of 64 threads over the flattened (position, head) rows, so each wave reads two heads = 1 KB contiguous of v_a and v_b, with a row >= P*H guard for odd totals (P*H passed as an appended argument). The arithmetic is the baseline's unchanged (true division kept), so results match within the battery without relying on tolerance.

friction: The reference timing drifted between runs from 0.1039 to 0.1122 ms (reference_headroom reported as 1.12, 1.15, 1.16, 1.17 and 1.21 for the same ref), so 60-pair speedups against ref are not comparable across candidates: block 128 measured 1.079 against ref but 0.988 against block 64 in a direct compare. The same state 465fdc7b495abe86 measured 1.060 at 60 pairs and 1.041 at 240 pairs. A bench that times several candidates against ref in one interleaved process would rank a sweep in one job.

compare() returns no traffic / headroom and does not record a verdict on the state, so states ranked only by compare (a555001fc25d178b, a8699eecec3f6e77, 0faf110cac31237b) have no bench entry in list_states.

No machine-level edit was attempted: the block-64 listing is straight-line with all four loads issued before the first wait, and I saw nothing left for unroll_loads, later waits or wide loads to act on. I did not test that assumption with an edit.
The existing coarsen states in list_states carry no factor in the summary line (action is just `coarsen`), so I could not tell which factors had already been tried without opening each state.
lessons: fi_merge_state is a memory-bound elementwise kernel (270.5 MB read, 135.3 MB written, each element once; reference headroom 1.12 to 1.21). Best result 1.041x at 240 pairs, ending at headroom about 1.10; consistent with the notes that kernels at headroom 1.0 to 1.2 gain a few percent at most.

What paid was launch geometry alone: flattening block (32, H) with one workgroup per position (16 waves per workgroup at H=32) into one-wave workgroups of 64 threads over flattened rows, each wave reading 1 KB contiguous per input. Block sweep on the flattened source against ref at 60 pairs: 64 -> 1.065, 128 -> 1.079 (noisy ref run), 256 -> 1.041, 1024 -> 0.999 (parity). Direct compare at 240 pairs put block 128 at 0.988 of block 64.

Replacing two IEEE divisions (v_div_scale / v_div_fmas / v_div_fixup sequences, about 25 VALU instructions) with one v_rcp_f32 and two multiplies was parity on this kernel: 1.0043 in compare at 240 pairs (CI 0.9974 to 1.0094). Arithmetic is not the bound; keep the exact division and stay bit-compatible.
Reading the per-head scalars through wave-uniform scalar loads instead of per-lane 4-byte gathers of the same two addresses: parity (0.9949, CI 0.992 to 1.0027).

32 bytes per lane (2 KB contiguous per wave per tensor) lost 4 % against 16 bytes per lane (0.9587), and coarsen factor 2 on the one-wave block-64 state lost 2.6 % (0.9741). Both agree with the existing notes for fi_silu_and_mul and rb_nrm2.

60-pair timings against ref moved by 2 % for the same state between runs here (1.060 then 1.041 at 240 pairs) because the ref time itself drifted by up to 8 %; rank a sweep with compare at 240 pairs, not with separate benches against ref.

session.final:
The 1.5x target was not reached: the best verified state is `465fdc7b495abe86` at **1.041x** over amdclang (240 pairs, CI 1.0345 to 1.0496). It passes the static check and the full 77-case battery, and the report is filed with it as the state to ship.

This is the memory-bound case. amdclang's build already runs at 1.12 to 1.21 times the memory floor, and every tensor element is touched exactly once, so there are no re-reads to remove. The shipped state ends at about 1.10 times the floor.

**What the winning state does:** it replaces one workgroup per position (block `(32, H)`, 16 waves at H=32) with one-wave workgroups of 64 threads over the flattened (position, head) rows. Each wave reads two heads, 1 KB contiguous from each input. A guard on `row >= P*H` handles odd totals, and the arithmetic is the baseline's unchanged, including the true division.

**What did not help on top of it:**

| Idea | Result against the block-64 state |
|---|---|
| Reciprocal instead of the two divisions | parity (1.004) |
| Scalar loads for the per-head scalars | parity (0.995) |
| Block 128 | 0.988 |
| 32 bytes per lane | loss (0.959) |
| `coarsen` factor 2 | loss (0.974) |

Against amdclang, block 256 was 1.041x and block 1024 was parity. I stopped after three ideas of different kinds each brought less than 1 %.

I made no machine-level edits. The block-64 listing is straight-line with all four loads issued before the first wait, and I saw nothing left for the passes to act on, but I did not test that with an edit.

The reference timing drifted by up to 8 % between runs, so 60-pair speedups against `ref` were not comparable across candidates. The same shipped state measured 1.060x at 60 pairs and 1.041x at 240; the harness's re-verification may land nearer the lower figure.
